questions.q: What does retiring an asset do?
options: Moves it to a new location
Permanently removes it (or a portion) from active, depreciating service
questions.explain: Retirement is the lifecycle stage where an asset is sold, scrapped, or otherwise permanently taken out of depreciating service.

questions.q: A 20-unit asset at $500/unit ($10,000 total) has 5 units retired by units. What cost is retired?
questions.explain: Retiring by units calculates proportional cost: $10,000 x (5/20) = $2,500.

questions.q: What happens to the remaining units after a partial retirement?
options: They continue depreciating normally, based on the reduced cost basis
They stop depreciating until the full asset is retired
They are transferred to a different book
questions.explain: In a partial retirement, only the retired portion leaves service; the remaining units keep depreciating on the asset's new, reduced cost basis.

questions.q: Which of these is captured as part of a retirement transaction?
options: Proceeds of sale and cost of removal
questions.explain: A retirement transaction captures retirement date, proceeds of sale, cost of removal, and a retirement type/reason — all feeding into the gain/loss calculation.

questions.q: What is the difference between retiring by cost and retiring by units?
options: They are identical; the names are interchangeable
Retiring by cost specifies a dollar amount directly; retiring by units specifies a count, with cost calculated proportionally
Retiring by units can only be used for CIP assets
Retiring by cost cannot be used for partial retirements
questions.explain: Retire by cost lets you specify the dollar amount directly, while retire by units lets you specify a unit count and the system calculates the proportional cost.
